newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton urges progress on trade rows with Japan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges progress on trade rows with Japan.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Sunday stressed the need to settle trade disputes with Japan over insurance and aviation that have been bedevilling relations between the two economic powers.

Clinton told Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in a meeting on the fringes of a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders in Manila that the row over deregulation of Japan's insurance market was their most important two-way trade problem, a Japanese official told reporters.
But he also asked for Japan's help in promoting an issue on which Washington and Japan see eye to eye -- a U.S. plan to axe tariffs on information technology by the turn of the century.

Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Clinton said Hashimoto assured him of Japan's desire to settle their trade disputes. Clinton also said that economic recovery in Japan would help ease problems such as Japan's chronic trade surplus.

"I think insurance is the most important one right now," the Japanese official quoted Clinton as telling Hashimoto. Clinton said it was "important to achieve results" on insurance and to make progress on another thorny dispute over aviation.
Washington has pressed Japan in meetings on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference here to resolve the insurance dispute by a December 15 deadline.

The dispute stems from U.S. charges that parts of the lucrative Japanese insurance market are closed to U.S. firms. The United States is opposed to Japn opening up a niche market for accident and health insurance, in which U.S. firms have a strong presence, before liberalising the wider market.

Clinton and Hashimoto also agreed to put their aviation talks on a higher level to speed a resolution of that dispute, the official said. The disagreement centres on an aviation pact dating from the 1950s which Japan says favours the United States. The two sides have agreed to re-start the aviation talks early next year.

Hashimoto also said it was important to resolve the issue of relocating a U.S. military air base from the Japanese island of Okinawa, the official said, while Clinton stressed the value of their security ties.

The two countries are due to hold talks in Tokyo about Okinawa on December 2. The issue flared up last year after the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen that fuelled local anger over the concentration of U.S. bases on Okinawa.
Clinton assured Hashimoto that the United States wanted improved ties with China and that the stability of China was important for the region, the Japanese official said.
Hashimoto said he welcomed a thaw in Sino-U.S. relations, crowned on Sunday when Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin agreed to an exchange of summit visits over the next two years.
The U.S.-Japan meeting did not touch on China's entry into the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which is expected to be high on the agenda of the APEC summit in Subic Bay north of Manila on Monday.

The Japanese official said Clinton asked for Hashimoto's support in promoting the U.S. plan for an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) after APEC ministers showed only muted support for the idea in their pre-summit meetings.
"I would like to ask for your cooperation over the wording of the ITA in the summit declaration," Clinton was quoted as telling Hashimoto.
Japan, as a major player in the computer market, supports the U.S. push for free trade in information technology.
